title: Manifolds And Smooth Maps
notes: Open the lecture by naming the chapter as the inspection kit for the rest of differential topology. The source span runs from pages 1 through 56, but the working story is compact: put coordinates on a space, differentiate maps between spaces, and use rank conditions to decide which geometric features survive.

title: A Chapter Built Around Rank
notes: Use the route diagram as a dependency map rather than a table of contents. Charts make derivatives meaningful, derivatives expose rank, the inverse function theorem explains full rank, and the one-sided rank cases lead to immersions, submersions, transversality, Sard theorem, Morse functions, and embeddings.

title: Charts Are Local Measuring Devices
notes: Stress that a manifold is not a preferred coordinate grid. A chart is a temporary measuring device, and the overlap maps are the real compatibility test. Once the overlap maps are smooth, calculus done in one coordinate window translates coherently to calculus done in another.

title: Tangent Vectors Live Before Coordinates
notes: Present the tangent vector first as a direction that differentiates functions, then as a coordinate column only after a chart is chosen. This avoids the common misconception that the tangent space is literally the ambient picture; the diagram only records one faithful local measurement.

title: The Differential Is The Local Linear Model
notes: Make the derivative the central instrument of the chapter. A smooth map may be globally curved and folded, but at a point it sends infinitesimal source directions to infinitesimal target directions by a linear map. Rank, kernel, and image are the data read from that local model.

title: Full Rank Gives Local Invertibility
notes: Explain the inverse function theorem as a local statement, not a global promise. When the derivative is an isomorphism, nearby coordinates can be chosen so the map is reversible near the point. The global map may still fail to be one-to-one or onto elsewhere.

title: Immersions Keep Source Directions Distinct
notes: Use the curve picture to separate three ideas that are often blended together. An immersion only requires the differential to be injective at every point. An embedding asks for the map to identify the source with its image topologically as well as smoothly, which rules out hidden self-overlap.

title: Submersions Produce Regular Level Sets
notes: For a scalar map, a nonzero differential means the kernel is a codimension-one tangent direction. The level set is then locally a smooth slice. Emphasize the practical test: regular values are values where every point in the preimage has full target rank.

title: Constant Rank Gives Normal Forms
notes: Connect the inverse, immersion, and submersion theorems through one organizing principle. If the rank is constant near a point, suitable source and target coordinates make the map look like a coordinate projection with inactive coordinates. The geometry is in the stable rank.

title: Transversality Is The Rank Test For Meetings
notes: Frame transversality as the condition that two tangent descriptions jointly fill the ambient tangent space. A transverse intersection is stable under small perturbations because the missing directions are supplied. A tangency is fragile because both objects try to move through the same infinitesimal channel.

title: Sard Theorem Makes Regular Values Abundant
notes: State the conceptual role of Sard theorem without dwelling on the measure proof. Critical values may be complicated, but they occupy a negligible part of the target. Therefore regular values are not rare accidents; they are plentiful enough to support generic constructions.

title: Morse Functions Stabilize Critical Points
notes: Move from regular values to controlled critical points. A Morse critical point has an invertible Hessian in local coordinates, so the function looks quadratically stable near that point. On a compact manifold, such functions give a manageable finite diagnostic for topology.

title: Embeddings Need Separation As Well As Rank
notes: Return to the distinction between local and global tests. Rank detects whether a map is locally faithful on tangent directions, but it does not by itself prevent distant points from colliding. Embedding arguments add separation data so the smooth model is a genuine copy.

title: A Smooth Map Diagnostic
notes: Use this slide as a repeatable workflow for students. First choose local coordinates, then compute the differential, read the rank condition, decide whether the local model is inverse, immersed, submersed, or transverse, and finally test whether global embedding or genericity requirements remain.

title: Common Failure Modes
notes: The warning slide is meant to reduce overgeneralization. Coordinates can hide the invariant object, full-rank conclusions are local, transversality is stronger than nonempty intersection, Sard theorem says almost every value is regular rather than every value, and embeddings require topology as well as injective derivative.

title: What To Carry Forward
notes: Close by tying the chapter to later differential topology. The remaining course repeatedly asks the same questions in harder settings: choose charts, compute derivatives, read rank, perturb toward transversality, pick regular values, and use embeddings or Morse functions to make topology visible.
